title: Pentagon Reportedly Weighed Wartime Powers to Reinstate Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

Senior Pentagon officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg, reportedly considered invoking the Defense Production Act (DPA) to pressure Nvidia’s board of directors into reinstating Jensen Huang as chief executive officer.

The Washington Post reported the discussions on November 25, citing three people familiar with the matter. The Pentagon subsequently denied that such a proposal had been made.

Enacted in 1950 during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act provides the federal government with broad authority to prioritize industrial production in support of national defense.

Although the legislation does not explicitly authorize the government to appoint corporate executives, the reported discussions highlight the extraordinary strategic importance Nvidia has acquired within the United States.

Huang was reinstated on November 23 following his resignation earlier this month amid revelations concerning extramarital affairs. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance reportedly played significant roles in encouraging his return.

There is no public evidence that the Defense Production Act was invoked in connection with Huang’s reinstatement.

Why It Matters
Nvidia has become far more than a semiconductor company. Its graphics processors, networking technologies and software ecosystem provide critical infrastructure for artificial intelligence, scientific computing, national laboratories and defense-related research.

The reported discussions underscore how the global AI race, particularly competition between the United States and China, is increasingly blurring the boundaries between commercial technology leadership and national security.

They also raise significant questions about corporate governance, board independence, government intervention and executive accountability.

For the semiconductor industry, this episode illustrates the growing geopolitical importance of advanced computing infrastructure and the risks associated with concentrating technological leadership around individual executives.

Ultimately, Nvidia's leadership controversy demonstrates how closely semiconductor manufacturing, artificial intelligence, financial markets and national security have become intertwined.
